title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 25
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Two Wheels, Late
passages.text:
A. The bicycle is a puzzle in the history of technology because nothing in it required materials or knowledge unavailable centuries earlier. Wheels, bearings, chains and tubular frames were all within reach of workshops that never produced one. The delay was not technical scarcity but the absence of an idea — that a vehicle could be inherently unstable and yet controllable by its rider — which nobody had reason to entertain until someone demonstrated it.

B. Early designs were propelled by the rider's feet against the ground and had no pedals at all. They were dismissed as a novelty, and the dismissal was reasonable, since on the rutted surfaces of the period they were slower and more exhausting than walking. What they established was the balance principle, and that established idea outlived the machines that demonstrated it.

C. Pedals attached directly to the front wheel produced the shape most people picture, and its enormous front wheel was not a stylistic choice but arithmetic. One turn of the pedals meant one turn of the wheel, so speed depended on the wheel's circumference, and the wheel grew until it reached the limit of the rider's leg length. The result was fast, expensive and dangerous, and it confined cycling to young men who could afford to fall.

D. The chain drive undid all of that at once. Separating pedalling rate from wheel size allowed small equal wheels, a low frame and a stable machine that an ordinary person could mount, and the pneumatic tyre made it tolerable on real roads. The combination is the machine still in use, and it arrived as a package whose parts were individually unremarkable.

E. Its social effects were disproportionate to its mechanical simplicity and were noticed at the time. It gave independent mobility at a cost within reach of working incomes, and it did so for women in particular at a moment when their movement was closely supervised. The dress reform that cycling required was contested precisely because everyone understood that the argument was not about clothing.

F. Its later trajectory shows how thoroughly infrastructure determines use. Where roads were rebuilt around motor vehicles the bicycle became marginal and was recast as a child's toy or a sporting object; where separated networks were maintained or restored it remained ordinary adult transport. The same machine, in countries of comparable wealth, accounts for a few per cent of journeys or a quarter of them depending on what was built around it.

passages.title: The Chemistry of Standing Still
passages.text:
A plant cannot run, and everything about how it survives being eaten follows from that. It must tolerate attack, deter it, or arrange for something else to intervene, and the machinery for all three is chemical. A substantial fraction of the compounds a plant produces has no role in growth or reproduction at all and exists to affect other organisms — a category that includes most of what humans use plants for.

The deterrent chemistry works by cost rather than by lethality. Compounds that make tissue bitter, indigestible or mildly toxic do not need to kill an animal to be effective; they need only make that plant a worse option than the next one, and an animal with alternatives will move on. This explains why so many defensive compounds are unpleasant rather than dangerous, and why the same compound can be a spice, a medicine and a poison depending entirely on quantity.

Production is expensive, which is why much of it is switched on only when needed. Damage to leaf tissue triggers signalling that raises defensive compound production both at the wound and in undamaged leaves elsewhere on the plant, and a plant that has been attacked once responds faster and more strongly to a second attack. The resemblance to immunity is real at the level of behaviour, though the mechanisms have nothing in common.

Recruiting other organisms is the most striking strategy and the least intuitive. Damaged plants release volatile compounds that attract predatory and parasitic insects to the herbivores eating them, effectively summoning enemies of the enemy. Whether neighbouring plants that detect these volatiles and increase their own defences are being warned is disputed; the more parsimonious reading is that they are eavesdropping on a signal not addressed to them, which requires no cooperation to explain.

Human agriculture has systematically removed this chemistry, and the reason is straightforward: the compounds that deter insects mostly taste bad to people too. Domesticated crops are typically less defended than their wild relatives, and the resulting vulnerability is one reason cultivation depends so heavily on applied protection. Efforts to breed defence back in run into the original problem, which is that the plant's chemical arsenal and human palatability point in opposite directions.

The pharmacological consequence is that the plant kingdom is a library of compounds evolved specifically to be biologically active in animals. That is why so many drugs originate in plants and why so many traditional remedies contain something real, and it is equally why plant-derived does not mean gentle. A compound produced to disable a caterpillar's nervous system is not safe by virtue of its origin, and dose remains the whole of the argument.

passages.title: Keeping the Lights On
passages.text:
An electricity grid has an unusual physical requirement that shapes its entire economics: supply and demand must match continuously, second by second, because the system stores almost nothing. Every other commodity market can absorb a mismatch through inventory. Electricity cannot, and the entire apparatus of grid operation exists to maintain a balance that would otherwise fail within seconds.

This requirement explains why generating capacity is built that is expected to sit idle almost all the time. Demand peaks are brief and predictable in shape, and meeting them requires plant that runs for a few dozen hours a year, whose cost must nonetheless be recovered. A market that paid only for energy delivered would not fund it, which is why most systems pay separately for availability — an arrangement that looks like paying for nothing and is paying for the ability to avoid a failure.

Adding wind and solar changes the problem in a way frequently misdescribed. Their output varies with weather rather than with demand, and the resulting difficulty is not that they are unreliable in the ordinary sense — their output is forecastable with reasonable accuracy — but that the system must be able to cover the periods when they produce little, which occur regardless of how much capacity has been built. Doubling wind capacity does not halve the length of a still week.

The economic consequence is more interesting than the engineering one. Wind and solar have negligible running costs, so they displace fuel-burning plant whenever they run, and in doing so they reduce the number of hours over which the displaced plant recovers its fixed costs. The plant that the system still needs for the still week becomes less viable precisely as more renewable capacity is added, which is why energy-only markets have been modified almost everywhere renewables have grown substantially.

Storage is described as the solution more often than the evidence supports, and the reason is a confusion of timescales. Batteries are excellent at seconds-to-hours problems — smoothing, frequency response, shifting an evening peak — and that is a genuinely valuable service. Covering a week of low wind is a different problem by three orders of magnitude, and the technologies that might do it are either geographically constrained, expensive per unit of energy stored, or not yet built at scale.

The options for that residual problem are unglamorous and mostly involve not solving it with generation at all. Interconnection borrows from places where the weather differs; demand response pays consumers to want less at the difficult moments; and retaining some firm capacity for rare use accepts that a system with very high renewable output still needs something that works irrespective of weather. Every serious plan uses a combination, and the argument is about proportions rather than about which single answer is correct.
